summaries.gardner: BHP is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: a 140-year-old miner of index-priced commodities in mature industries with no product advantage that consumers notice. It does have strong recent price momentum (about +47% over 52 weeks) and a copper-growth story, but it lacks the emerging-industry leadership and unique innovation Gardner looks for.
summaries.buffett: BHP owns irreplaceable, low-cost assets and produces large free cash flow ($11,929M in FY2026), but Buffett generally avoids commodity producers whose earnings swing with prices they cannot control. At about 21.6 times FY2026 diluted earnings ($83.29 per ADS against $3.864 diluted EPS per ADS), there is no obvious margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the cornered-resource quality of Escondida and the Pilbara and the conservative balance sheet (net debt $8.7bn, 0.3x EBITDA). Inverting, though, there are several ways to lose: commodity price falls, Chinese buyer power, project overruns such as Jansen Stage 2, and legal liability from the Mariana dam failure.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms BHP is a cyclical that is also trying to become a copper stalwart; with cyclicals the trick is buying when P/E looks high near the bottom and selling when it looks low near the top. At a P/E of about 21.6 against 8.9% diluted EPS growth in FY2026, the PEG test fails, and the stock is widely followed rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's 15 points favour companies with growing products, R&D and sales skill; BHP's growth comes from developing new mines (Jansen potash, Escondida concentrator, Vicuña) rather than new products. Its management depth and operating culture are strong, but sales skill and R&D-driven growth are not a source of advantage in commodities.
summaries.graham: BHP passes Graham's size, financial-strength, dividend-record and earnings-growth tests (positive profit every year FY2017-FY2026, diluted EPS up from $1.104 in FY2017 to $1.932 in FY2026), but fails his price tests: about 23.7 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B of about 90, far above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: BHP has no proprietary technology and sells undifferentiated commodities in competitive markets, so it fails most of Thiel's seven questions; its 'monopoly-like' feature is ownership of rare, low-cost deposits. Its distribution to Asian steelmakers and smelters is solid, and its copper position should still hold in 20 years.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders tied to big secular shifts at reasonable prices; BHP's copper exposure ties it to electrification and grid build-out, but revenue is forecast to be roughly flat in FY2027-FY2029. It is a disciplined, profitable operator, but not the kind of high-growth tech compounder he usually backs.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller's macro approach could favour BHP in a copper up-cycle, and the share price is up about 47% over 52 weeks, with underlying profit up 30% in FY2026. However, consensus has FY2027 revenue slightly down and copper output guided lower (1,650-1,800 kt), so earnings momentum is not clearly accelerating from here.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical commodity producers because they lack pricing power and consistent high returns; BHP's 26.1% underlying ROCE in FY2026 is good, but it has swung with the cycle, including a statutory loss in FY2016. BHP would not fit Fundsmith's 'good companies' screen.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula BHP scores reasonably: operating profit of $23,869M is about 10.6% of an enterprise value of roughly $225.6bn, and underlying ROCE was 26.1% in FY2026. Greenblatt's formula would rank it decently, though cyclical peak-ish earnings can flatter both measures.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, great managers and great reinvestment; BHP has good managers and some high-return reinvestment (Escondida, Copper South Australia), but commodity price dependence and the Jansen Stage 2 cost rise from $4.9bn to $6.9bn weaken the 'great business' and reinvestment legs.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary trouble at deep discounts with low downside; BHP is simple and financially strong, and its China iron ore dispute was resolved in April 2026. But after a 47% rally and at about 21.6 times earnings, it is not trading at a distressed price.
summaries.wood: BHP does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation focus: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics. It is at most an indirect supplier of copper for electrification.
summaries.ackman: Ackman's criteria favour simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and little exposure to outside forces; BHP is simple and dominant in copper and iron ore but highly exposed to commodity prices, which conflicts with his predictability requirement.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model needs a business that passes its cost savings to customers to build an ever-wider moat; BHP sells at market prices and keeps its cost advantage as margin. Its long-life assets are durable, but the flywheel he sought is absent.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with technology; BHP is a mature incumbent miner in established commodity markets, so his venture framework barely applies. The only fit is the size of the markets it serves.
summaries.nash: Tom Nash explicitly avoids commodity producers, and BHP also fails his kill test on more debt ($27,121M of interest-bearing liabilities) than cash ($18,532M) at June 30, 2026, and on his DCF, which gives about $55 per ADS against an $83.29 price. Its Nash-style score is about 65 of 130, below the 75 bar, despite a 40.6% operating margin.

momentum.evidence: BHP's NYSE ADR closed at $83.29 on October 16, 2026, up about 46.7% over 52 weeks according to StockAnalysis.

g4.evidence: CEO Brandon Craig is a respected 25-year BHP operator, and BHP partners with Lundin Mining (Vicuña) and Global Infrastructure Partners ($2.0bn for 49% of a WAIO power partnership), but it is not backed by famous growth investors.

g6.evidence: The consensus rating is 'Hold' with an average 12-month target of $77.92, below the $83.29 price, so some analysts see it as fully valued.

simple.evidence: BHP digs copper, iron ore and coal out of the ground and sells them at market prices; FY2026 revenue was 49% copper, 41% iron ore and 10% coal.

b2.evidence: Profit attributable to shareholders was positive every year from FY2017 to FY2026, but it swung from $30,900M in FY2022 to $7,897M in FY2024, and FY2016 was a loss year.

integrity.evidence: BHP has a clear capital allocation framework (minimum 50% payout, 72% in FY2026, net debt $8.7bn below its target range), but the Mariana dam failure led to an English High Court finding of liability that BHP was refused permission to appeal in 2026.

b6.evidence: BHP twice approached Anglo American (2024 and November 2025) before walking away, showing both deal appetite and discipline; the new CEO says a deal must be 'incredibly compelling' to beat organic options.

roic.evidence: Underlying ROCE was 26.1% in FY2026 with net debt only 0.3x EBITDA, but returns rise and fall with commodity prices.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 operating cash flow of $21,778M less $9,849M of PP&E purchases gives $11,929M, more than statutory attributable profit of $9,833M.

b10.evidence: Retained profits funded high-return copper and iron ore assets, but past reinvestment destroyed value (the US shale foray, and a $2.3bn Jansen impairment in FY2026).

safety.evidence: A Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount rate gives about $55 per ADS, below the $83.29 price, and the price is above the $77.92 average analyst target.

fairprice.evidence: About 21.6 times FY2026 diluted earnings and a 5.6% FCF yield is fair for a low-cost miner near good copper prices, but not cheap with revenue forecast flat.

mu5.evidence: With low debt and tier-one assets, BHP is unlikely to fail, but earnings can fall sharply through commodity price falls, Chinese buyer pressure, cost overruns or large dam-related damages.

reinvest.evidence: BHP says its pipeline could lift copper output about 40% by FY35 and Escondida earns a 53% ROCE, but new projects such as Jansen Stage 2 (now $6.9bn) earn far lower returns.

ly2.evidence: BHP is a classic cyclical, with a copper-led growth story: copper contributed more than half of Underlying EBITDA for the first time in FY2026.

ly3.evidence: P/E of about 21.6 is far above FY2026 diluted EPS growth of 8.9% ($1.774 to $1.932).

runway.evidence: Copper growth (Escondida new concentrator, Vicuña, Resolution) and Jansen potash add volume over the next decade, but analysts see revenue roughly flat through FY2029.

ly7.evidence: Diluted weighted shares edged up from 5,083M in FY2025 to 5,089M in FY2026, there is no buyback, and insiders hold about 0.03%.

ly8.evidence: BHP is one of the world's largest miners (market capitalisation about $212bn) and is covered by many analysts.

fi2.evidence: BHP is adding a new commodity, potash, with Jansen Stage 1 due in mid-CY2027, and developing new copper districts as older mines deplete.

fi3.evidence: BHP does not report a material R&D line; its innovation is in operating technology such as autonomous haulage, whose returns are not separately disclosed.

fi4.evidence: Its products sell at index-linked prices, and it had to concede terms to China's CMRG after a ban on several products from September 2025 to April 2026.

longterm.evidence: BHP is investing in decades-long projects like Jansen (expected to operate for more than 60 years) and Escondida's new concentrator rather than maximising short-term payouts.

gr1.evidence: FY2026 revenue was $58,760M and total assets $121,387M.

ni10.evidence: Attributable profit was positive every year FY2017-FY2026, from $3,705M in FY2018 (the lowest) to $30,900M in FY2022; FY2016, eleven years ago, was a loss year.

gr4.evidence: BHP has paid dividends every year for decades, including a $1.72 per share total for FY2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.104 in FY2017 to $1.932 in FY2026, up 75% (FY2016 was a loss year).

gr6.evidence: $83.29 per ADS is about 23.7 times the FY2024-FY2026 average diluted EPS of $3.51 per ADS.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 21.6 times price-to-book of about 4.2 (book equity attributable to shareholders of $50,923M, about $20.04 per ADS) is about 90.

th1.evidence: BHP has no proprietary product technology; its edge is low-cost orebodies.

timing.evidence: Electrification and grid investment support copper demand now, while China's steel slowdown weighs on iron ore and coal.

th3.evidence: BHP grew through mergers (notably BHP Billiton in 2001) in large established markets, not from a dominant share of a small niche.

team.evidence: BHP has a deep, experienced operating management team led by career insider Brandon Craig, but no exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: BHP has long-standing marketing relationships and logistics (rail and ports) to deliver ore to Asian steel mills and smelters.

durable.evidence: Long-life deposits like Escondida, the Pilbara and Jansen (60+ year life) and the need for copper make its position likely to hold in 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Copper and potash growth are well known, and rivals (Rio Tinto, Anglo Teck, Nutrien) are pursuing them too.

trend.evidence: As the world's largest copper producer (about 2 Mt in FY2026), BHP benefits from electrification and AI data-centre power build-out, but indirectly.

dr1.evidence: Underlying attributable profit rose 30% to $13.2bn in FY2026, but consensus FY2027 revenue of $57.96B is about 1.4% below FY2026.

dr2.evidence: Jansen Stage 1 first production in mid-CY2027 and the WAIO path above 305 Mtpa are positives, offset by lower FY2027 copper guidance (1,650-1,800 kt).

dr4.evidence: Lower rates and infrastructure spending support copper demand, while China's weak property sector holds back iron ore.

dr6.evidence: First potash from Jansen in mid-CY2027, Escondida's new concentrator decision (CY2027-28) and copper price moves could lift results.

dr7.evidence: With revenue forecast flat and the share price above the average analyst target, conviction is not high enough for a concentrated position.

gm.evidence: BHP reports no gross margin; its 59% Underlying EBITDA margin reflects low costs and high copper prices rather than pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $11,929M is about 5.6% of the roughly $211.6bn market capitalisation, reasonable for a mature miner.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 profit from operations of $23,869M is about 10.6% of an enterprise value of about $225.6bn.

pa2.evidence: The CMRG iron ore ban was lifted in April 2026, but the China steel slowdown and lower copper grades are more lasting.

pa4.evidence: Net debt of $8.7bn (0.3x EBITDA), $18,532M of cash and tier-one assets make permanent loss unlikely, though a cyclical drawdown is possible.

wo1.evidence: BHP is a miner, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: Mining costs don't fall quickly with volume; FY2027 Escondida unit costs are guided up to $1.20-1.50/lb from $1.07/lb.

wo3.evidence: BHP does not combine innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its commodity markets grow modestly; analysts expect revenue of $58,510M in FY2029, about the same as FY2026.

ac3.evidence: Results depend directly on copper, iron ore and coal prices; revenue swung from $65,098M in FY2022 to $51,262M in FY2025.

ns1.evidence: BHP sells at index prices and keeps its cost advantage as margin rather than sharing it with customers.

ns4.evidence: Copper growth and potash diversification could strengthen it by 2036-2046, but iron ore and coal may shrink.

va2.evidence: It supplies copper and iron ore, which the world needs for power grids, electric vehicles and steel.

tn1.evidence: Copper is infrastructure for electrification and AI power demand, but BHP is a traditional miner adapting its portfolio, not a company built for that trend.

tn2.evidence: BHP is often seen as an iron ore miner, while copper made up more than half of Underlying EBITDA for the first time in FY2026.

tn3.evidence: BHP is a commodity producer, one of Nash's zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable ($9,833M attributable in FY2026), but revenue fell in FY2025 and debt ($27,121M) exceeds cash ($18,532M).

tn5.evidence: BHP reports half-yearly; free cash flow was positive ($11,929M in FY2026), but interest-bearing liabilities have exceeded cash at each balance-sheet date.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 14.6% plus an FCF margin of 20.3% is about 35, below 40.

tn9.evidence: It hits the 'more debt than cash' kill ($27,121M vs $18,532M).

tn10.evidence: BHP faces the English group action over the 2015 Fundão (Mariana) dam collapse: it was found liable, refused permission to appeal in 2026, and a damages trial starts in April 2027.

tn11.evidence: BHP provides copper, iron ore and coal that help steelmakers and smelters make steel and metal, and charges index-linked commodity prices; customers choose it for reliable, large-scale, low-cost supply.

tn13.evidence: Total about 65/130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return 0 (not verified), moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn20.evidence: BHP reports half-yearly, and no reliable record of beats versus consensus was verified.

tn22.evidence: BHP has $58,760M of revenue, is profitable, has no ongoing share sales, and is not a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At 3.4% average revenue growth and a 19.9% FCF margin the DCF gives about $55 per ADS, so the $83.29 price implies more growth than BHP is delivering.
